2 / Boards and what they do

Who decides, who moves, who signs.

Brain

Raspberry Pi 4, 4 GB

Runs Raspberry Pi OS 64-bit, the Grablab agent, the two camera streams, the NFC reader and peaqOS. Decides every move, reads every sensor, signs every event. Own official 5.1 V 3 A supply. Ethernet, not Wi-Fi.

Motion

Arduino UNO + CNC Shield V3

GRBL firmware, flashed once. The Pi sends G-code over USB ("go to X350 Y420"), the UNO turns it into step pulses for four A4988 drivers: X, Y left, Y right (slot A cloned from Y) and the Z winch. Three endstops give the home position.

Claw

L298N H-bridge

Takes 12 V and two direction pins from the Pi. Pushes the 12 V linear actuator in the claw out (fingers open) or in (fingers closed). The actuator stops itself at both ends. Power travels through the drag chain and the coil cable.

Identity

OPTIGA Trust M Express

Security chip on a Shield2Go board, I2C address 0x30. The machine's private key is generated inside and can never be read out. It signs the peaq verification and every drop proof. The only chip profile peaqOS Verify accepts.

Power

12 V 10 A supply, E-stop, Wago

230 V in through the Qoltec cable, 12 V out. The E-stop's NC contact sits in series on 12 V +, so pressing it stops motors, claw and servo at once. Two 5-way Wago 221 blocks distribute + and -. The Pi stays on.

5 V rail

Buck 12 V to 5 V, 3 A

Sealed module, nothing to adjust. Feeds only the MG90S servo that releases the capsule. The servo must never draw from the Pi's 5 V pins.

Drop sensor

E3JK-5DM2-5L through beam

Emitter and receiver in drop-in cradles on the printed seat, the beam across the 45 mm ball where it rests. 12 V powered. The receiver's relay contact closes when a ball breaks the beam, so the Pi reads a clean, isolated contact.

Capsule ID

ACR122U NFC reader

USB NFC reader in the slide-in cradle under the printed seat. Reads the NTAG215 UID of the ball resting tag down on the seat, twice, before the gate may open. No GPIO, no I2C, just USB.

Eyes

Two 1080p USB webcams

Front camera on the front top tube, side camera inside under the right top tube. Together they stream the whole floor to the player. Both USB, H.264 encoded on the Pi.

3 / Raspberry Pi pin map

Ten wires, one loom.

Make the Pi loom as one Dupont bundle in a textile sleeve, labelled at both ends. Physical pin numbers in brackets. Everything on the GPIO is 3.3 V logic; nothing from the 12 V side touches a GPIO pin directly.

4 / OPTIGA Trust M in the system

The key never leaves the chip.

The OPTIGA is a small secure element wired to the Pi over I2C. The Pi asks it to sign things; it never gets to see the private key. peaqOS trusts a signature from this chip as proof that the data came from this physical machine. Two flows use it: once at onboarding (Verify), then on every grab.

What ends up on chain is the keccak256 hash of drop.json and the machine id. Anyone can recompute the hash from the raw data we publish and compare. The chip signature inside the JSON ties the data to this exact machine; the Verify record ties this machine to its DID.

Verify accepts exactly one chip profile: infineon-optiga-trust-m-express-ca306/1, which is the TRUSTMEXPSHIELDTOBO1 board. No TPM, no software key, no other Trust M variant. The challenge comes from peaq's onboarding service with a token we get from the peaq team, not from the machine.

For Aethelark

What the build has to deliver

The shield mounted inside the Pi case on two M3 screws, four Dupont wires (3V3, GND, SDA, SCL, 10 cm), and i2cdetect -y 1 showing 30. Nothing else. Software, keys and peaq onboarding are Grablab's side.

Why inside the case

Possession is part of the proof

Whoever holds the chip can sign as the machine. It lives inside the cabinet, inaccessible without opening it, and the Pi case lid is screwed shut. Do not leave the chip on a breadboard or outside the panel.

Tools on the Pi

linux-optiga-trust-m, peaq-os-cli

Infineon's tools compiled on the Pi; trustm_cert -r 0xe0e0 -o leaf.pem must work before anything else. peaq-os-cli 0.0.14 or newer, Python 3.10+, clock synced with NTP. No ROS 2 needed for identity or events.

6 / Rules, budget and open items

Things that must stay true.

Grounds

Bonded once

12 V minus, the buck's minus and the Pi ground meet at one point: the GND Wago block, reached from the Pi through the single GND wire of the loom to the L298N logic header. Never add a second bond; it makes a loop that corrupts the I2C and the sensor reads.

E-stop

Cuts 12 V, never the Pi

NC contact in series on 12 V + before the Wago block: motors, actuator, servo and sensor all drop. The Pi keeps running, sees the NO contact on GPIO16 and logs the stop. Mains stays under the printed cover with the supply.

Current budget

About 7 A worst case

Four NEMA 17 at 1.0 A set on the A4988 (Vref 0.8 V with 0.1 ohm sense resistors, check the module) make 4 A peak, the actuator 1 A, the buck under 1 A, the sensor 0.1 A. In practice the motors average under 2 A. The 10 A supply has margin.

Connectors

No bare strands, no solder

Ferrules on every wire that enters a screw terminal or a Wago. Crimped Dupont on the boards. Motor cables plug into the shield as they come. The coil cable's two pairs are doubled, two wires per actuator pole.

Open item

peaq onboarding token

The Verify challenge needs a token operators don't hold. Grablab is asking the peaq team. The machine is fully wirable and testable without it; only the "verified" badge waits for it.

Open item

Inline fuse on 12 V +

The BOM has no fuse between the supply and the E-stop. We recommend an 8 A blade fuse holder on 12 V + right after the supply. Cheap, local, and it protects the Wago wiring if the actuator ever stalls hard.

Production notes

What changes later

Cytron MD10C replaces the L298N (no 2 V drop), an industrial Omron beam replaces the Heschen pair, a Pi 5 with NVMe replaces the Pi 4 and the microSD when the machine runs 24/7. None of this changes the wiring tree.
